# DHIS2 Modeling

Chap (the Chap Modeling Platform) runs climate and health forecasting models, evaluates them and connects them to DHIS2 through the DHIS2 Modeling App. A Chap model is a train script and a predict script in R or Python, plus an MLproject file that describes them. It is evaluated locally with `chap eval --run-config.as-chapkit`, from the `chap-core` package (`uv tool install chap-core`), and deployed as a chapkit Docker image. A model developer does not install chapkit separately, does not run the chap-core `docker compose` stack and does not need `chapkit mlproject migrate`. Start with "Getting started as a model developer" and "Bring your existing model to Chap".

# Model developers

# Getting started as a model developer

The Chap platform brings several advantages to you as a model developer:

- It provides a [broad range of supporting functionality for modelling](https://chap.dhis2.org/chap-modeling-platform/external_models/supporting_functionality/index.md), allowing you to focus on what is unique in your project, while relying on Chap for data parsing, model tuning, rigorous model assessment and more.
- It allows you to evaluate your model [side-by-side with a range of other models](https://chap.dhis2.org/chap-modeling-platform/external_models/side_by_side_comparison/index.md) in the field
- It comes with [native connection to DHIS2 and the DHIS2 Modelling App](https://chap.dhis2.org/chap-modeling-platform/external_models/chap-dhis2-connection/index.md), and includes mechanisms to disseminate your model to a large number of health ministries that use DHIS2 as their national health information system.

## How a model runs in Chap

A Chap model is a train script and a predict script, in R or Python, plus a short `MLproject` file that tells Chap how to run them. Once your model is Chap-compatible, you can use it in two ways:

- **On your own machine**, with the `chap` command-line tool. One command evaluates the model on a dataset and plots its forecasts:

  ```console
  chap eval --model-name . --dataset-csv data.csv --output-file eval.nc --plot --run-config.as-chapkit
  ```

- **In the Chap Modeling App**, where users can evaluate it on DHIS2 data, compare it with other models and make forecasts. For this, you package the model as a Docker image and add it to a Chap installation, see [Running Your Own Model](https://chap.dhis2.org/chap-modeling-platform/modeling-app/running-your-own-model/index.md).

## Where to start

First [set up your machine](https://chap.dhis2.org/chap-modeling-platform/external_models/setup/index.md). Then pick the guide that fits you:

| You...                                                                | Start here                                                                                                                         |
| --------------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| already have a forecasting model in R or Python                       | [Bring your existing model to Chap](https://chap.dhis2.org/chap-modeling-platform/external_models/existing_model/index.md)         |
| want to build a new model                                             | [Build a new model from a template](https://chap.dhis2.org/chap-modeling-platform/external_models/mlproject_tutorial/index.md)     |
| are not used to the terminal, git, or installing Python or R packages | [Development tools](https://chap.dhis2.org/chap-modeling-platform/external_models/development_tools/index.md), then come back here |
| want to learn statistical modelling and forecasting                   | [Learning modelling](https://chap.dhis2.org/chap-modeling-platform/external_models/learn_modelling/index.md)                       |

Both model guides use the same `MLproject` format and the same `chap eval` command. They only differ in where you start: from your own code, or from a template.

Strictly, Chap only requires that a model exposes the chapkit REST API. The train and predict scripts and the `MLproject` file are the recommended way to get there, since chapkit then provides the API for you. Advanced users can write a service that implements the API directly, see the [chapkit documentation](https://dhis2-chap.github.io/chapkit/). Most models do not need this.

# Set up your machine

This page lists what you need to develop a model and evaluate it with Chap on your own machine. You do not need a Chap server, a database, the Modeling App or a separate chapkit install.

If the terminal, git or package managers are new to you, read [Development tools](https://chap.dhis2.org/chap-modeling-platform/external_models/development_tools/index.md) first.

## Windows: use WSL

Chap runs on macOS and Linux. On Windows, install WSL2 (Windows Subsystem for Linux) and run every command on these pages in the WSL terminal. See [Chap on Windows](https://chap.dhis2.org/chap-modeling-platform/external_models/prepare-for-installation/#chap-on-windows).

## 1. Install uv

Chap is installed with [uv](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/), a tool for installing Python programs and packages. You need it even if your model is written in R.

macOS:

```console
brew install uv
```

Linux and WSL:

```console
curl -LsSf https://astral.sh/uv/install.sh | sh
```

Close and reopen the terminal, then check that it works:

```console
uv --version
```

## 2. Install Chap

```console
uv tool install chap-core --python 3.13
```

This installs the `chap` command. uv puts Chap and the packages it uses (more than a hundred) in a folder of their own, so the install does not change your other Python projects or your R setup. Check that it works:

```console
chap --help
```

To update Chap later, run `uv tool upgrade chap-core`.

## 3. Install your model's language

- **R models:** install [R](https://cran.r-project.org/), and check that `Rscript --version` works in the terminal. RStudio is optional.
- **Python models:** nothing more is needed. uv can install Python for your model.

## 4. Docker (only to deploy)

You do not need Docker to develop or evaluate a model. You need it when you package the model so that it can run next to a Chap installation. On macOS and Windows, install [Docker Desktop](https://docs.docker.com/desktop/). On Linux, install [Docker Engine](https://docs.docker.com/engine/install/).

## Next

- [Bring your existing model to Chap](https://chap.dhis2.org/chap-modeling-platform/external_models/existing_model/index.md)
- [Build a new model from a template](https://chap.dhis2.org/chap-modeling-platform/external_models/mlproject_tutorial/index.md)

# Bring your existing model to Chap

This guide is for you if you already have a forecasting model in R or Python and want to run it in Chap. You keep your code. The guide has three stages:

1. **Run the model outside Chap.** Split it into a train and a predict script that read and write Chap's data format, and check that they work on example data.
1. **Make it Chap-compatible.** Add a short `MLproject` file and evaluate the model with `chap eval`.
1. **Package it as a Docker image**, so that it can run next to a Chap installation.

You only need Docker for the last stage.

What you do not need

- **No separate chapkit install.** Installing Chap also installs chapkit, and `chap eval` starts and stops the chapkit service for you. There is no `brew install chapkit`.
- **No Chap server.** You do not need to clone chap-core or run its `docker compose up`. That stack runs Chap for the Modeling App, and is not needed to develop or evaluate a model.
- **No `chapkit mlproject migrate`** and no `main.py`. They turn a model into a chapkit service project with its own service code, which most models do not need.

If you do not have a model yet, see [Build a new model from a template](https://chap.dhis2.org/chap-modeling-platform/external_models/mlproject_tutorial/index.md) instead.

Train and predict scripts are a recommendation, not a requirement

The only strict requirement is that your model exposes the chapkit REST API, which Chap uses to send it data and get forecasts back. The train and predict scripts and the `MLproject` file in this guide are the easiest way to get there: chapkit reads them and provides the API for you. If you are comfortable writing a web service, you can implement the API yourself instead, in any language. See the [chapkit documentation](https://dhis2-chap.github.io/chapkit/) and its [API reference](https://dhis2-chap.github.io/chapkit/guides/ml-workflows/#api-reference).

## Before you start

Follow [Set up your machine](https://chap.dhis2.org/chap-modeling-platform/external_models/setup/index.md). You need `chap` installed, and R if your model is in R.

The [R template](https://github.com/chap-models/mlproject_template_r) and the [Python template](https://github.com/chap-models/mlproject_template_python) contain a small model that is already set up the way this guide describes. Keep the one for your language open: you will copy files from it.

## 1. Run the model outside Chap

### Split the model into a train and a predict script

Chap runs your model as two commands:

- **train** reads a CSV file with historic data and saves a trained model to a file.
- **predict** loads the trained model, reads the historic data and a CSV file with climate data for the future periods, and writes the forecasts to a CSV file.

Chap passes the file paths as command-line arguments. The templates show the smallest version of this: [train.r](https://github.com/chap-models/mlproject_template_r/blob/main/train.r) and [predict.r](https://github.com/chap-models/mlproject_template_r/blob/main/predict.r) in R, [train.py](https://github.com/chap-models/mlproject_template_python/blob/main/train.py) and [predict.py](https://github.com/chap-models/mlproject_template_python/blob/main/predict.py) in Python.

The input CSV files have the columns `time_period`, `location` and `disease_cases`, plus the covariates your model uses, such as `rainfall`, `mean_temperature` and `population`. See [Chap data format](https://chap.dhis2.org/chap-modeling-platform/external_models/prepare_data/index.md). The future data has the same columns, but no `disease_cases`.

The predict script writes a CSV file with `time_period`, `location` and the forecast in a `sample_0` column, one row per location and future period. A model that gives several samples writes `sample_1`, `sample_2` and so on.

### Run the scripts on example data

Copy the template's `input` folder, with [trainData.csv](https://github.com/chap-models/mlproject_template_r/blob/main/input/trainData.csv) and [futureClimateData.csv](https://github.com/chap-models/mlproject_template_r/blob/main/input/futureClimateData.csv), into your model's folder. Then run the scripts. For R:

```console
mkdir -p output
Rscript train.R input/trainData.csv output/model.bin
Rscript predict.R output/model.bin input/trainData.csv input/futureClimateData.csv output/predictions.csv
```

Open `output/predictions.csv` and check that it has a `sample_0` column.

If R says `there is no package called 'xgboost'` (or another package), install the package and run again:

```console
Rscript -e 'install.packages("xgboost")'
```

For a Python model, install the packages it needs in a virtual environment, and keep that environment active in the terminal for this stage and the next. See [Virtual environments](https://chap.dhis2.org/chap-modeling-platform/kigali-workshop/kigali-webinar-series/session-2/virtual-environments/index.md) if this is new to you.

The templates have an `isolated_run` script that runs both steps. You can copy it and change the file names to make reruns quicker.

## 2. Make the model Chap-compatible

### Write the MLproject file

Create a file named `MLproject` (no file extension) in your model's folder. For an R model:

```yaml
name: my_model

required_covariates:
  - rainfall
  - mean_temperature

entry_points:
  train:
    parameters:
      train_data: str
      model: str
    command: "Rscript train.R {train_data} {model}"
  predict:
    parameters:
      historic_data: str
      future_data: str
      model: str
      out_file: str
    command: "Rscript predict.R {model} {historic_data} {future_data} {out_file}"
```

For a Python model, the commands are `python train.py ...` and `python predict.py ...`.

- `name` is a short name for your model, without spaces.
- `required_covariates` lists the dataset columns the model reads, besides `time_period`, `location` and `disease_cases`. Chap checks that a dataset has them before it runs the model.
- `command` is what Chap runs. Chap replaces the `{...}` placeholders with file paths. Use these names, since they are the ones Chap knows: `train_data`, `historic_data`, `future_data`, `model` and `out_file`. Put them in the order your scripts expect.

The file has no line that says how to install the model's packages. For now, the model runs with the R or Python and the packages you already have. You add that line at the end of this stage.

If your `MLproject` already has a `docker_env`, `conda_env` or `python_env` line, Chap cannot use it to run the model as a chapkit service. Remove the line, or keep it and add `--run-config.ignore-environment` to the `chap eval` command below.

### Evaluate the model with Chap

From your model's folder, run:

```console
chap eval --model-name . --dataset-csv https://raw.githubusercontent.com/dhis2-chap/chap-core/master/example_data/laos_subset.csv --output-file eval.nc --plot --run-config.as-chapkit --run-config.ignore-environment
```

- `--model-name .` means the model in the current folder.
- `--dataset-csv` is the data to evaluate on. The example is monthly data for a few provinces in Laos. You can also use your own data in the [Chap data format](https://chap.dhis2.org/chap-modeling-platform/external_models/prepare_data/index.md).
- `--run-config.as-chapkit` runs the model the same way a Chap server will run it.
- `--run-config.ignore-environment` runs the scripts with the R or Python and the packages you already have, as in stage 1.

Chap trains and tests the model on several periods of the data (a backtest) and writes the results to `eval.nc`. `--plot` writes a plot of the forecasts against the real case counts to `eval.html`. Open it in a browser.

### If something goes wrong

- **A package is missing:** install it as in stage 1 and run `chap eval` again.
- **A required covariate is missing:** the dataset does not have a column your `MLproject` lists under `required_covariates`. Use a dataset that has it, or remove it from the list if the model does not need it.
- **Running an MLproject with docker_env as a chapkit service is not supported:** see the end of [Write the MLproject file](#write-the-mlproject-file).
- **Something else:** add `--run-config.debug` to the `chap eval` command to see the output of your scripts.

### Record the model's packages

To run anywhere other than your machine, the model has to say which packages it needs. Add a line to the `MLproject` that Chap uses to install them:

- **R:** record the packages with [renv](https://rstudio.github.io/renv/) (`renv::init()`, then `renv::snapshot()`) and add `renv_env: renv.lock`.
- **Python:** list the packages in a `pyproject.toml` with uv (`uv init`, then `uv add <package>`) and add `uv_env: pyproject.toml`.

Run `chap eval` again without `--run-config.ignore-environment`. Chap now installs the packages itself before it runs the model. The Docker image in the next stage installs them the same way.

## 3. Package the model as a Docker image

To run next to a Chap installation, the model is packaged as a Docker image. You need [Docker](https://chap.dhis2.org/chap-modeling-platform/external_models/setup/#4-docker-only-to-deploy) for this stage.

Let an AI coding agent do the work

AI coding agents, such as Claude Code, Codex or GitHub Copilot, are now good at making an existing model Chap-compatible, both stage 2 and this stage. Open the agent in your model's folder and point it to a model that already works with chapkit, and to the documentation. With an agent, you often do not need to do much by hand. For example:

> Make this model Chap-compatible, following https://chap.dhis2.org/chap-modeling-platform/external_models/existing_model/. Use https://github.com/chap-models/mlproject_template_r as the example to copy from: add an `MLproject` file, record the packages with renv, and add the `Dockerfile`, `.dockerignore`, `compose.yml` and GitHub workflows. Then check that `chap eval --run-config.as-chapkit` works on the example data.

Use [mlproject_template_python](https://github.com/chap-models/mlproject_template_python) for a Python model. The [chapkit documentation](https://dhis2-chap.github.io/chapkit/), and its [MLproject runner guide](https://dhis2-chap.github.io/chapkit/guides/mlproject-runner/) in particular, are also useful to give the agent. Check what the agent changed, and run `chap eval` yourself before you publish the model.

Copy these files from the template for your language into your model's folder:

| File                                   | What it does                                                                                                                                              | R                                                                                                                        | Python                                                                                                                        |
| -------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `Dockerfile`                           | Builds the image from a chapkit base image that runs the `MLproject` as a chapkit service, and installs the packages from `renv.lock` or `pyproject.toml` | [Dockerfile](https://github.com/chap-models/mlproject_template_r/blob/main/Dockerfile)                                   | [Dockerfile](https://github.com/chap-models/mlproject_template_python/blob/main/Dockerfile)                                   |
| `.dockerignore`                        | Keeps local files such as your installed packages and `output/` out of the image                                                                          | [.dockerignore](https://github.com/chap-models/mlproject_template_r/blob/main/.dockerignore)                             | [.dockerignore](https://github.com/chap-models/mlproject_template_python/blob/main/.dockerignore)                             |
| `compose.yml`                          | Builds and starts the image with one command                                                                                                              | [compose.yml](https://github.com/chap-models/mlproject_template_r/blob/main/compose.yml)                                 | [compose.yml](https://github.com/chap-models/mlproject_template_python/blob/main/compose.yml)                                 |
| `.github/workflows/ci.yml`             | Tests the image on GitHub                                                                                                                                 | [ci.yml](https://github.com/chap-models/mlproject_template_r/blob/main/.github/workflows/ci.yml)                         | [ci.yml](https://github.com/chap-models/mlproject_template_python/blob/main/.github/workflows/ci.yml)                         |
| `.github/workflows/publish-docker.yml` | Publishes the image on GitHub                                                                                                                             | [publish-docker.yml](https://github.com/chap-models/mlproject_template_r/blob/main/.github/workflows/publish-docker.yml) | [publish-docker.yml](https://github.com/chap-models/mlproject_template_python/blob/main/.github/workflows/publish-docker.yml) |

To download them all at once, run this in your model's folder. For R:

```console
mkdir -p .github/workflows && for f in Dockerfile .dockerignore compose.yml .github/workflows/ci.yml .github/workflows/publish-docker.yml; do curl -fsSL -o $f https://raw.githubusercontent.com/chap-models/mlproject_template_r/main/$f; done
```

For Python, replace `mlproject_template_r` with `mlproject_template_python`.

The R `Dockerfile` expects the `renv.lock`, `.Rprofile` and `renv/` folder that `renv::init()` created in stage 2. The Python one expects the `pyproject.toml` that `uv init` created.

In `compose.yml`, you can rename the service from `mlproject_template_r` or `mlproject_template_python` to your model's name. Then build the image and start it:

```console
docker compose up --build
```

The model is now at http://localhost:9090. In another terminal, check that Chap can use it:

```console
chap eval --model-name http://localhost:9090 --run-config.is-chapkit-model --dataset-csv https://raw.githubusercontent.com/dhis2-chap/chap-core/master/example_data/laos_subset.csv --output-file eval.nc
```

### Publish the image

GitHub builds and publishes the image for you every time you push to the `main` branch. If your model is not on GitHub yet, create a new, empty repository on GitHub and push your folder to it, see [Git and GitHub](https://chap.dhis2.org/chap-modeling-platform/kigali-workshop/kigali-webinar-series/session-2/git-github/index.md). Then commit the new files and push them:

```console
git add -A && git commit -m "Package the model as a Docker image" && git push
```

On GitHub, the **Actions** tab of your repository shows the workflows building, testing and publishing the image as `ghcr.io/<your-user>/<your-repo>:latest`. See [Publish the image](https://chap.dhis2.org/chap-modeling-platform/external_models/mlproject_tutorial/#publish-the-image) in the template tutorial for what to check there.

## Next steps

- Run the model from the Chap modeling app, see [Running Your Own Model](https://chap.dhis2.org/chap-modeling-platform/modeling-app/running-your-own-model/index.md).
- Make parts of the model configurable with `user_options`, see [Model Configuration Options](https://chap.dhis2.org/chap-modeling-platform/external_models/additional_configuration/#model-configuration-options).
- Add author and contact details, see [Model Metadata](https://chap.dhis2.org/chap-modeling-platform/external_models/model_metadata/index.md).

# Build a new model from a template

This tutorial takes you from a template to your own model running in Chap. You write a train and a predict script, in R or Python, and a short `MLproject` file that describes them. Chap runs the model as a [chapkit](https://chap.dhis2.org/chap-modeling-platform/external_models/chapkit/index.md) service, but you do not write any service code.

What you do not need

- **No separate chapkit install.** Installing Chap also installs chapkit, and `chap eval` starts and stops the chapkit service for you. There is no `brew install chapkit`.
- **No Chap server.** You do not need to clone chap-core or run its `docker compose up`. That stack runs Chap for the Modeling App, and is not needed to develop or evaluate a model.
- **No `chapkit mlproject migrate`** and no `main.py`. They turn a model into a chapkit service project with its own service code, which most models do not need.

If you already have a model, follow [Bring your existing model to Chap](https://chap.dhis2.org/chap-modeling-platform/external_models/existing_model/index.md) instead.

The tutorial starts from one of two template repositories:

- [mlproject_template_python](https://github.com/chap-models/mlproject_template_python), using uv for dependencies
- [mlproject_template_r](https://github.com/chap-models/mlproject_template_r), using renv for dependencies

Both contain the same model: a linear regression from rainfall and temperature to disease cases in the same month. The model is not meant to be good. It only shows the steps.

The tutorial has three stages:

1. **Run the model outside Chap** on example data, while you develop it (steps 1 to 3).
1. **Evaluate it with Chap** (step 4).
1. **Package it as a Docker image** and publish it, so that it can run next to a Chap installation (step 5).

## Requirements

Follow [Set up your machine](https://chap.dhis2.org/chap-modeling-platform/external_models/setup/index.md). You need `chap` and, for the R template, R. Docker is only needed for the last step, deploying the model.

## 1. Create your repository from the template

Make your own copy of the template on GitHub, so that you can change it and push your changes:

1. Open the [Python template](https://github.com/chap-models/mlproject_template_python) or the [R template](https://github.com/chap-models/mlproject_template_r) on GitHub.

1. Click **Use this template**, then **Create a new repository**. Give it a name, for example `my_model`. GitHub creates `https://github.com/<your-user>/my_model`.

1. Clone your copy, with your GitHub user name and the name you chose:

   ```console
   git clone https://github.com/<your-user>/my_model
   cd my_model
   ```

Your copy has everything the tutorial needs, including the files that build and publish the Docker image in step 5. You do not need to write those yourself. If git and GitHub are new to you, see [Git and GitHub](https://chap.dhis2.org/chap-modeling-platform/kigali-workshop/kigali-webinar-series/session-2/git-github/index.md).

## 2. The files

| File                                 | Purpose                                                                                               |
| ------------------------------------ | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `train.py` / `train.r`               | Reads the training data and saves a trained model to a file                                           |
| `predict.py` / `predict.r`           | Loads the trained model and writes forecasts for the future periods                                   |
| `MLproject`                          | Tells Chap how to run the scripts, which covariates the model uses, and how to set up its environment |
| `pyproject.toml` / `renv.lock`       | The model's dependencies                                                                              |
| `isolated_run.py` / `isolated_run.r` | Runs train and predict on the example data, without Chap                                              |
| `Dockerfile`                         | Packages the model as a chapkit service                                                               |
| `compose.yml`                        | Builds and starts the Docker image with one command                                                   |
| `.github/workflows/`                 | Test the Docker image and publish it when you push to GitHub                                          |
| `input/`                             | A small example dataset                                                                               |

The Python `MLproject` looks like this:

```yaml
name: mlproject_template_python

meta_data:
  display_name: MLproject Template (Python)
  description: Linear regression from rainfall and temperature to disease cases. A starting point for new models.

required_covariates:
  - rainfall
  - mean_temperature

uv_env: pyproject.toml

entry_points:
  train:
    parameters:
      train_data: str
      model: str
    command: "python train.py {train_data} {model}"
  predict:
    parameters:
      historic_data: str
      future_data: str
      model: str
      out_file: str
    command: "python predict.py {model} {historic_data} {future_data} {out_file}"
```

- `required_covariates` lists the dataset columns the model reads, besides `time_period`, `location` and `disease_cases`. Chap checks that a dataset has them before it runs the model.
- `uv_env` (or `renv_env: renv.lock` in the R template) says how to set up the model's environment.
- `entry_points` are the commands for training and predicting. Chap fills in the `{...}` placeholders with file paths. Use these parameter names, since they are the ones Chap knows: `train_data`, `historic_data`, `future_data`, `model`, `out_file`, and optionally `model_config` and `polygons`.

The data format is described in [Chap data format](https://chap.dhis2.org/chap-modeling-platform/external_models/prepare_data/index.md). The predict script writes one row per location and future period, with the forecast in a `sample_0` column. A model that gives several samples writes `sample_1`, `sample_2` and so on.

## 3. Run the model without Chap

Develop and debug the model on the example data first.

**Python:**

```console
uv run python isolated_run.py
```

uv installs the packages listed in `pyproject.toml` the first time.

**R:**

```console
Rscript -e "renv::restore()"
Rscript isolated_run.r
```

The first command installs the packages listed in `renv.lock`.

Both scripts train the model on `input/trainData.csv`, saves it in `output/` and writes forecasts for `input/futureClimateData.csv` to `output/predictions.csv`.

Edit the scripts and rerun until the model does what you want. To add a dependency, add it to `pyproject.toml` (Python), or install it with `renv::install("pkg")` and record it with `renv::snapshot()` (R). If the model reads new dataset columns, add them to `required_covariates`.

## 4. Evaluate the model with Chap

From the template directory, run:

```console
chap eval --model-name . --dataset-csv input/trainData.csv --output-file output/eval.nc --plot --run-config.as-chapkit
```

Chap copies the model to a run directory, sets up its environment (`uv sync`, or `renv::restore()`), starts it as a chapkit service on a free local port, runs a backtest against it, and stops the service. The results are in `output/eval.nc`, and `--plot` writes an HTML plot next to it.

The example dataset is small and synthetic. For a more realistic run, use a dataset such as `example_data/laos_subset.csv` from the [chap-core repository](https://github.com/dhis2-chap/chap-core). `--model-name` also accepts a GitHub URL, so others can evaluate your model without cloning it. See the [eval command reference](https://chap.dhis2.org/chap-modeling-platform/chap-cli/eval-reference/#running-an-mlproject-as-a-chapkit-service) for all options.

To make parts of the model configurable, for example the number of lags, declare `user_options` in the `MLproject`. See [Model Configuration Options](https://chap.dhis2.org/chap-modeling-platform/external_models/additional_configuration/#model-configuration-options). Other fields you can set, such as author and contact details, are listed in [Model Metadata](https://chap.dhis2.org/chap-modeling-platform/external_models/model_metadata/index.md).

## 5. Package the model as a Docker image

To run next to a Chap installation, the model is packaged as a Docker image. Your repository already has the files for this, so there is nothing to write: `Dockerfile` describes the image, `compose.yml` builds and starts it, and the workflows in `.github/workflows` build and publish it on GitHub. You need [Docker](https://chap.dhis2.org/chap-modeling-platform/external_models/setup/#4-docker-only-to-deploy) for this step.

### Build and test the image on your machine

From your repository folder, run:

```console
docker compose up --build
```

The first build takes a few minutes. The model is then at http://localhost:9090. In another terminal, check that Chap can use it:

```console
chap eval --model-name http://localhost:9090 --run-config.is-chapkit-model --dataset-csv input/trainData.csv --output-file output/eval.nc
```

Stop it with `Ctrl+C`, or `docker compose down`.

What the Dockerfile does

It starts from a chapkit base image that runs an `MLproject` as a chapkit service, installs your dependencies, and copies your scripts in unchanged. The Python one installs the dependencies from `pyproject.toml`:

```dockerfile
FROM ghcr.io/dhis2-chap/chapkit-py-cli:latest
WORKDIR /work
COPY pyproject.toml ./
RUN uv pip install --python /app/.venv/bin/python -r pyproject.toml
COPY . .
```

The R one restores the packages in `renv.lock`:

```dockerfile
FROM ghcr.io/dhis2-chap/chapkit-r-cli:latest
WORKDIR /work
COPY .Rprofile renv.lock ./
COPY renv/ renv/
RUN Rscript -e "renv::restore(prompt = FALSE)"
COPY . .
```

The dependencies are installed before the scripts are copied, so editing a script does not reinstall them. There are also base images with the tidyverse or INLA preinstalled, see [Running in a container](https://dhis2-chap.github.io/chapkit/guides/mlproject-runner/#running-in-a-container) in the chapkit docs.

### Publish the image

GitHub builds and publishes the image for you every time you push to the `main` branch. Commit your changes and push them:

```console
git add -A && git commit -m "Update the model" && git push
```

Then follow the build on GitHub:

1. Open your repository on GitHub and click the **Actions** tab. Two workflows run for your push:
   - **CI** builds the image, starts it and runs `chap eval` against it.
   - **Publish Docker image** publishes the image.
1. When both have a green check mark, the image is published as `ghcr.io/<your-user>/<your-repo>:latest`. It is listed under **Packages** on the right side of your repository's front page.
1. The first time, open the package and check its visibility. If it is private, change it to public under **Package settings**, so that a Chap installation can pull it.

To publish a fixed version as well, push a tag such as `v1.0.0`: `git tag v1.0.0 && git push --tags`. The image then also gets the tag `1.0.0`.

If a workflow fails, click it to see which step failed and its output.

To use the model from the Chap modeling app, run the image next to Chap. The service registers itself with Chap on startup. See [Running Your Own Model](https://chap.dhis2.org/chap-modeling-platform/modeling-app/running-your-own-model/index.md).

## Next steps

- If you need service logic that an `MLproject` cannot express, `chapkit mlproject migrate` turns the repository into a full chapkit project with a generated `main.py`. See [MLproject Migrate](https://dhis2-chap.github.io/chapkit/guides/mlproject-migrate/) in the chapkit docs.
- [Chapkit](https://chap.dhis2.org/chap-modeling-platform/external_models/chapkit/index.md) describes the data Chap sends to a chapkit service.

# Additional Configuration

Some additional model configuration must be specified, and some fields are optional. This will be explained below and it is relevant for both Python and R models.

## Specifying prediction length constraints

Include `min_prediction_length` and `max_prediction_length` in your model configuration to define how many time periods your model can predict ahead. When users need predictions beyond your `max_prediction_length`, Chap automatically uses ExtendedPredictor to make iterative predictions (see [supporting functionality](https://chap.dhis2.org/chap-modeling-platform/external_models/supporting_functionality/index.md)).

## Model Configuration Options

You can define configurable parameters in your MLproject file using `user_options`. This allows users to customize model behavior when running your model, without modifying the model code itself.

### Schema structure

Each option in `user_options` has the following fields:

- `title`: Display name for the parameter
- `type`: One of `string`, `integer`, `number`, `boolean`, or `array`
- `description`: What the parameter does
- `default`: Optional default value. If omitted, the parameter is required

### Example MLproject with user_options

```yaml
name: my_model

docker_env:
  image: python:3.11

entry_points:
  train:
    parameters:
      train_data: str
      model: str
    command: "python train.py {train_data} {model}"
  predict:
    parameters:
      historic_data: str
      future_data: str
      model: str
      out_file: str
    command: "python predict.py {model} {historic_data} {future_data} {out_file}"

user_options:
  n_lag_periods:
    title: n_lag_periods
    type: integer
    default: 3
    description: "Number of lag periods to include in the model"
  learning_rate:
    title: learning_rate
    type: number
    description: "Learning rate for training (required)"
```

### Providing configuration values

Configuration values can be provided via the `--model-configuration-yaml` CLI flag when running `eval` or other commands:

```console
chap eval my_model data.csv results.nc --model-configuration-yaml config.yaml
```

The configuration YAML is a `ModelConfiguration` document with two top-level keys:

- `user_option_values` — a mapping whose keys must match the parameter names declared in your MLproject `user_options`
- `additional_continuous_covariates` — an optional list of extra continuous covariates (only meaningful when the template sets `allow_free_additional_continuous_covariates: true`)

```yaml
user_option_values:
  n_lag_periods: 5
  learning_rate: 0.01
additional_continuous_covariates:
  - rainfall
  - mean_temperature
```

### Validation rules

- The top-level YAML must contain only `user_option_values` and `additional_continuous_covariates`. Any other top-level key raises a validation error — flat YAMLs like `n_lag_periods: 5` at the root are rejected.
- Options without a `default` value are required and must be provided under `user_option_values`
- Only options defined in `user_options` are allowed under `user_option_values`
- Values must match the specified type (e.g., integers for `integer` type)

### Examples in the codebase

See the following example that uses `user_options`:

- [naive_python_model_with_mlproject_file_and_docker](https://github.com/dhis2-chap/chap-core/tree/master/tests/fixture_models/naive_python_model_with_mlproject_file_and_docker)

## Report Entry Point

In addition to the required `train` and `predict` entry points, a model may declare an optional `report` entry point that produces a PDF document describing the trained model (diagnostics, fitted-effect plots, posterior summaries, etc.). When defined, users can invoke it via the `chap report` CLI command.

### Adding a `report` entry point

Add a third entry to `entry_points` in `MLproject`. The entry point receives the same `historic_data` and `model` files as `predict`, plus an `out_file` path the model must write the PDF to:

```yaml
entry_points:
  train:
    parameters:
      train_data: str
      model: str
    command: "python train.py {train_data} {model}"
  predict:
    parameters:
      historic_data: str
      future_data: str
      model: str
      out_file: str
    command: "python predict.py {model} {historic_data} {future_data} {out_file}"
  report:
    parameters:
      historic_data: str
      model: str
      out_file: str
    command: "python report.py {model} {historic_data} {out_file}"
```

If the model has user options, declare `model_config: str` in the `report` parameters too — it is forwarded the same way as for `train`/`predict`.

### Contract

- The `model` parameter is the trained-model artifact written by `train`.
- The `historic_data` parameter is a CSV in the standard Chap format.
- The script must write a PDF to `out_file`. Chap does not validate the contents.
- `polygons.geojson` is not passed to `report`.

Models without a `report` entry point are still valid — `chap report` will return an error message naming the model.

## Simulate Entry Point

A model may declare an optional `simulate` entry point that generates disease data from covariates alone. Chap passes it a CSV with the covariates for a set of locations and periods, and the script writes the same rows back with the target column (`disease_cases` by default) filled in. Users invoke it via the `chap simulate` CLI command, and the output can be passed straight to `chap eval`.

```yaml
entry_points:
  simulate:
    parameters:
      covariates: str
      out_file: str
      model_config: str
    command: "python simulator.py simulate {covariates} {out_file} {model_config}"
```

### Continuing a simulation

The covariate CSV may already contain the target for some rows, for example the output of last week's simulation with new covariate rows appended. Those rows are observed history: the model must leave them unchanged and simulate only the rows where the target is missing. Chap rejects output that changes an observed value or leaves a value missing.

`model_config` is optional and is forwarded the same way as for `train`/`predict`, so simulation parameters can be declared as `user_options`. `{polygons}` is passed if the dataset has a GeoJSON file.

`train` and `predict` are still required in `MLproject`. A simulation-only model can point them at a command that raises an error. See [chap-models/climate_simulation_model](https://github.com/chap-models/climate_simulation_model) for a minimal example.

# Chap's native connection to DHIS2 and the DHIS2 Modelling App

Chap comes with native connection to DHIS2 and the DHIS2 Modelling App as described on the [main DHIS2 climate web page](https://dhis2.org/climate/)

# Examples of chap eval commands

The following are examples of running various chap-integrated models on various datasets:

- minimalist_example_r: `chap eval --model-name https://github.com/dhis2-chap/minimalist_example_r --dataset-csv https://raw.githubusercontent.com/dhis2/climate-health-data/refs/heads/main/lao/chap_LAO_admin1_monthly.csv --output-file eval.nc --plot --run-config.debug --backtest-params.n-splits 2`
- minimalist_multiregion_r: `chap eval --model-name https://github.com/dhis2-chap/minimalist_multiregion_r --dataset-csv https://raw.githubusercontent.com/dhis2/climate-health-data/refs/heads/main/lao/chap_LAO_admin1_monthly.csv --output-file eval.nc --plot --run-config.debug --backtest-params.n-splits 2`
- minimalist_example_lag_r: `chap eval --model-name https://github.com/dhis2-chap/minimalist_example_lag_r --dataset-csv https://raw.githubusercontent.com/dhis2/climate-health-data/refs/heads/main/lao/chap_LAO_admin1_monthly.csv --output-file eval.nc --plot --run-config.debug --backtest-params.n-splits 2`
- Madagascar_ARIMA: `chap eval --model-name https://github.com/chap-models/Madagascar_ARIMA --dataset-csv https://raw.githubusercontent.com/dhis2/climate-health-data/refs/heads/main/lao/chap_LAO_admin1_monthly.csv --output-file eval.nc --plot --run-config.debug --backtest-params.n-splits 2`
- Epidemiar: `chap eval --model-name https://github.com/chap-models/epidemiar_example_model --dataset-csv ../epidemiar_example_data/input/laos_test_data.csv --output-file eval.nc --plot --run-config.debug --backtest-params.n-splits 2`
- chap_auto_ewars_weekly: `chap eval --model-name https://github.com/chap-models/chap_auto_ewars_weekly --dataset-csv https://raw.githubusercontent.com/dhis2/climate-health-data/refs/heads/main/lao/chap_LAO_admin1_monthly.csv --output-file eval.nc --plot --run-config.debug --backtest-params.n-splits 1`
- chap_auto_ewars: `chap eval --model-name https://github.com/chap-models/chap_auto_ewars --dataset-csv https://raw.githubusercontent.com/dhis2/climate-health-data/refs/heads/main/lao/chap_LAO_admin1_monthly.csv --output-file eval.nc --plot --run-config.debug --backtest-params.n-splits 1`

Note that the Epidemiar command uses a local file path for the supplied dataset as it requires weekly data. The command above works when cloning the epidemiar_example_model locally and if the command is run from the folder chap-core, then it assumes that the cloned repository is in the same folder as chap-core, and we use the relative file path. You can also simply download the csv file laos_test_data.csv from the github folder and reference the path to the local file.

chap_auto_ewars only accepts monthly data while chap_auto_ewars_weekly can use both weekly and monthly data, should be combined together soon. Additionally there is a version of chap_auto_ewars which uses spatial smoothing and a geojson file which can be ran as * `chap eval --model-name https://github.com/Halvardgithub/chap_auto_ewars --dataset-csv ../chap_auto_ewars/example_data_Viet/historic_data.csv --output-file eval.nc --plot --run-config.debug --backtest-params.n-splits 1` The above uses local files and their relative paths, the files are available at the github url.

## For Windows users

Windows users might have issues with the commands above. The solution is to clone the repositories for the external models and add the optional command `--run-config.run-directory-type use_existing`. An example is shown below. * minimalist_example_r: `chap eval --model-name /mnt/c/Users/NAME/Documents/GitHub/minimalist_example_r/ --dataset-csv https://raw.githubusercontent.com/dhis2/climate-health-data/refs/heads/main/lao/chap_LAO_admin1_monthly.csv --output-file eval.nc --plot --run-config.debug --backtest-params.n-splits 2 --run-config.run-directory-type use_existing`

Note that you need to use your own local file path, and if you are using WSL and ubuntu this might be with `mnt` from linux, even on a Windows system.

### Warnings

When running the command with a local file path for the model folder you can in theory run the command from any folder, not just from chap-core. However, running `chap eval` with `--run-config.run-directory-type use_existing` from the same folder as you are using as the `--model-name` will cause an infinite copying loop. Sometimes, if a command fails, it might be necessary to exit and open the folder again, for example run `cd ../chap-core` to go one folder up and then back to chap-core. Additionally, having an active VPN can also confuse Chap and cause the commands to fail.

# Running models with chapkit

Chapkit is one of two ways chap runs models. Chap is gradually migrating models to chapkit; both chapkit and the older approach are supported.

In contrast to the older approach, where models are run directly through docker and pyenv wrappers inside chap, chapkit models are separate REST API services that chap interacts with through HTTP requests.

This has several advantages:

- There are no docker-in-docker problems where chap (which is inside docker) has to run docker commands to start model containers.
- We have a strict and clear API for how chap interacts with models, which makes it easier to develop and maintain.
- Models can easily be distributed through docker images or other means, as long as they implement the chapkit API. It is up to the model to define how it is deployed and run, but chapkit makes it easy to spin up a rest api and make a docker image for a model.

This document describes very briefly how to make a model compatible with chapkit, and how to use chapkit models in chap.

## How to make a model compatible with chapkit

The simplest way is to describe the model in an `MLproject` file and let chapkit serve it, with no service code. See [Bring your existing model to Chap](https://chap.dhis2.org/chap-modeling-platform/external_models/existing_model/index.md) or [Build a new model from a template](https://chap.dhis2.org/chap-modeling-platform/external_models/mlproject_tutorial/index.md). For writing a chapkit service directly, see the chapkit documentation: <https://dhis2-chap.github.io/chapkit/>.

### Three ways to make a model

|                                | MLproject, built-in Chap runner                                                                                                                                                  | MLproject served by chapkit (recommended)                                                                                                                                                                                                                    | chapkit service                                                                |
| ------------------------------ | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| **You write**                  | Train and predict scripts, and an `MLproject` file                                                                                                                               | The same files                                                                                                                                                                                                                                               | Train and predict code, a `main.py` that defines the service, and a Dockerfile |
| **How Chap runs it**           | Chap reads the `MLproject` and runs the train and predict commands itself                                                                                                        | chapkit reads the `MLproject` and serves the model as a REST service. Chap sends it data over HTTP                                                                                                                                                           | Your service runs on its own. Chap sends it data over HTTP                     |
| **Evaluate with**              | `chap eval --model-name <directory or GitHub URL>`                                                                                                                               | `chap eval --model-name <directory or GitHub URL> --run-config.as-chapkit`                                                                                                                                                                                   | `chap eval --model-name <service URL> --run-config.is-chapkit-model`           |
| **Add to a Chap installation** | Chap fetches the model from GitHub, see [Getting new models into the modeling app](https://chap.dhis2.org/chap-modeling-platform/modeling-app/managing-model-templates/index.md) | Run a Docker image built from a chapkit base image. It registers itself with Chap                                                                                                                                                                            | Run the service's Docker image. It registers itself with Chap                  |
| **Where to start**             | [Connect your model to the Chap standard](https://chap.dhis2.org/chap-modeling-platform/external_models/describe_model/index.md)                                                 | [Bring your existing model to Chap](https://chap.dhis2.org/chap-modeling-platform/external_models/existing_model/index.md) or [Build a new model from a template](https://chap.dhis2.org/chap-modeling-platform/external_models/mlproject_tutorial/index.md) | The [chapkit documentation](https://dhis2-chap.github.io/chapkit/)             |

The first two use the same `MLproject` format, so a model written for one usually runs with the other. The exception is the environment: chapkit sets up `uv_env` and `renv_env`, but not `docker_env`, `conda_env` or `python_env`. What differs is who runs the model: Chap itself, or chapkit as a separate service. The second and third run the same way in Chap. The difference is whether chapkit builds the service from your `MLproject`, or you write the service code. A model can move from the second to the third with `chapkit mlproject migrate`, see [MLproject Migrate](https://dhis2-chap.github.io/chapkit/guides/mlproject-migrate/) in the chapkit docs.

## Data format sent to chapkit models

Chap sends data to chapkit models via the REST API in a standardized format. The data is sent as JSON with a `columns` array and a `data` array (column-oriented format).

### Required columns

The following columns are always present in the training and prediction data:

| Column             | Description                                  |
| ------------------ | -------------------------------------------- |
| `time_period`      | Time period identifier (see format below)    |
| `location`         | Location identifier                          |
| `disease_cases`    | Number of disease cases (training data only) |
| `rainfall`         | Rainfall measurement                         |
| `mean_temperature` | Mean temperature                             |
| `population`       | Population count                             |

### Time period format

The `time_period` column uses ISO-like string formats:

**Weekly data:**

```text
2020-W01
2020-W02
2020-W52
2021-W01
```

The format is `YYYY-Wnn` where:

- `YYYY` is the ISO week year
- `W` indicates weekly data
- `nn` is the zero-padded week number (01-53)

**Monthly data:**

```text
2020-01
2020-02
2020-12
2021-01
```

The format is `YYYY-MM` where:

- `YYYY` is the year
- `MM` is the zero-padded month number (01-12)

### Example training data (weekly)

```json
{
  "columns": ["time_period", "location", "disease_cases", "rainfall", "mean_temperature", "population"],
  "data": [
    ["2020-W01", "district_a", 150, 45.2, 28.5, 50000],
    ["2020-W02", "district_a", 142, 52.1, 27.8, 50000],
    ["2020-W01", "district_b", 89, 38.7, 29.1, 35000],
    ["2020-W02", "district_b", 95, 41.3, 28.9, 35000]
  ]
}
```

### Example training data (monthly)

```json
{
  "columns": ["time_period", "location", "disease_cases", "rainfall", "mean_temperature", "population"],
  "data": [
    ["2020-01", "district_a", 580, 180.5, 28.2, 50000],
    ["2020-02", "district_a", 620, 165.3, 27.9, 50000],
    ["2020-01", "district_b", 340, 155.8, 29.0, 35000],
    ["2020-02", "district_b", 365, 148.2, 28.7, 35000]
  ]
}
```

### Run info

Along with the data, Chap sends a `run_info` object containing runtime parameters:

```json
{
  "prediction_periods": 3,
  "additional_continuous_covariates": ["humidity"]
}
```

| Field                              | Description                                      |
| ---------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------ |
| `prediction_periods`               | Number of future periods to predict              |
| `additional_continuous_covariates` | List of additional covariate columns in the data |

`run_info` is sent on both `$train` and `$predict`. At train time `prediction_periods` is the horizon the model is going to be asked for, clamped to the `min_prediction_periods` and `max_prediction_periods` the service declares; at predict time it is the length of the future frame. Chap leaves the field out when it does not know the horizon, and the service then falls back to the value in its stored configuration.

Chapkit resolves the horizon from `run_info` first, then the future frame, then the stored configuration, so your model reads it from `config.prediction_periods` as usual. This requires chapkit 2.1.0 or newer; older versions ignore `run_info` at train time. Chap sent the horizon as `prediction_length` before chapkit 2.1.0, and chapkit still accepts that spelling.

## How to run a chapkit model from the command line

To test that the model works with Chap, use the `chap eval` command. Give the model's container image with `docker://` in front, and Chap starts the image as a container for the duration of the command and removes it afterwards. This needs Docker.

**Example:**

First save this model configuration to a file called `testconfig.yaml`:

```yaml
user_option_values:
  max_epochs: 2
```

Then evaluate the chtorch model from its image:

```console
chap eval --model-name docker://ghcr.io/dhis2-chap/chtorch:chapkit2-8f17ee3 --dataset-csv https://raw.githubusercontent.com/dhis2/climate-health-data/refs/heads/main/lao/chap_LAO_admin1_monthly.csv --output-file eval.nc --plot --backtest-params.n-splits 2 --backtest-params.n-periods 3 --model-configuration-yaml testconfig.yaml
```

If the model is already running as a service, for example one you started yourself with `docker run -p 5001:8000 <image>`, give its URL instead and add `--run-config.is-chapkit-model`:

```console
chap eval --model-name http://localhost:5001 --run-config.is-chapkit-model --dataset-csv ./data.csv --output-file eval.nc
```

A model from [Chap Marketplace](https://chap-marketplace.dhis2.org) can also be set up once in a [Chap project](https://chap.dhis2.org/chap-modeling-platform/chap-cli/projects/#chap-marketplace-models), which stores its verified image so that `chap eval` runs without options.

## How to use chapkit models in chap with the modeling app

Model services from the [Chap Marketplace](https://chap-marketplace.dhis2.org) are installed with `chap-admin install-all`, which starts the services and registers their templates and configurations with chap, so they appear in the modeling app. See [Install the Models](https://chap.dhis2.org/chap-modeling-platform/modeling-app/fresh-installation/#5-install-the-models) for the commands.

To add a model service that is not in the marketplace, see [Running Your Own Model](https://chap.dhis2.org/chap-modeling-platform/modeling-app/running-your-own-model/index.md).

## Making a dataset Chap-compliant

To use your data with Chap, it must be provided as a CSV file that follows the format described below. A complete working example is available in [example_data/laos_subset.csv](https://github.com/dhis2-chap/chap-core/blob/master/example_data/laos_subset.csv).

### Required columns

Every dataset must contain these columns:

| Column          | Description                                            |
| --------------- | ------------------------------------------------------ |
| `time_period`   | Time period identifier (see format below)              |
| `location`      | Location identifier (e.g. district name or code)       |
| `disease_cases` | Number of observed disease cases (the target variable) |

### Covariate columns

Models declare which climate covariates they need (e.g. `rainfall`, `mean_temperature`). The CSV must include a column for each covariate required by the model you are running. Covariate columns must not contain missing or NaN values.

### Population column

Most models also require a `population` column with the population count for each location and time period. Check the model's documentation to confirm whether it is needed.

### Mapping custom column names

If your CSV uses different column names than those expected by a model, you can provide a JSON mapping file via the `--data-source-mapping` option instead of renaming columns. See the [eval command reference](https://chap.dhis2.org/chap-modeling-platform/chap-cli/eval-reference/#data-source-mapping) for details.

### Specific named fields

The table below summarises every column name that Chap recognises:

| Column              | Required        | Description                                                                                                                      |
| ------------------- | --------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `time_period`       | Yes             | Time period in ISO format                                                                                                        |
| `location`          | Yes             | Location identifier                                                                                                              |
| `disease_cases`     | Yes             | Observed case count (target)                                                                                                     |
| `population`        | Model-dependent | Population for the location                                                                                                      |
| *covariate columns* | Model-dependent | Climate/environmental covariates (e.g. `rainfall`, `mean_temperature`)                                                           |
| `target_masked`     | Never in input  | Added by Chap on datasets with masked periods; reserved, so input data may not contain it. See [Masked periods](#masked-periods) |

### Time period format

The `time_period` column uses:

- `YYYY-MM` format for monthly data (e.g., `2023-01`)
- `YYYY-Wnn` format for weekly data (e.g., `2023-W01`)

All time periods in a dataset must use the same frequency (do not mix monthly and weekly).

### Missing values

Different columns have different rules for missing (NaN) values:

| Column          | NaN allowed? | Notes                                                                                                                |
| --------------- | ------------ | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `time_period`   | No           | Every row must have a valid period                                                                                   |
| `location`      | No           | Every row must have a location                                                                                       |
| `disease_cases` | Yes          | Surveillance data may have gaps; Chap tolerates NaN in the target. NaN can also mean the period is masked, see below |
| Covariates      | No           | Climate/environmental columns must be fully observed                                                                 |
| `population`    | Yes          | Missing values are forward-filled by interpolation when present                                                      |

Chap does not perform imputation on covariates. If your data pipeline produces NaN values in covariate columns, those must be resolved before passing the CSV to Chap. Locations with missing covariate values will be rejected during dataset validation.

Every `(location, time_period)` combination in the dataset must be present as a row. Missing rows are not allowed -- if a location covers 12 months, it must have all 12 rows. Chap will raise an error if any location has fewer time periods than others.

### Masked periods

A dataset can have masked periods: stretches such as COVID years or a reporting outage that should not be used for training.

Masking deletes data

When a dataset with masked ranges is created through the API, `disease_cases` inside the masked periods is stored as empty and the submitted values are **deleted**. They cannot be recovered or unmasked later. This also applies to every prediction-setup run, which inherits the masked ranges of its backtest's dataset. To use those periods again, import the data again from its source without the range.

With `--data-configuration` on the command line the CSV file is left as it is and only the loaded copy is masked. Either way, this is what the model receives:

| Data the model receives                   | `disease_cases`                                 | `target_masked` |
| ----------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------- | --------------- |
| Training and historic data, masked period | NaN                                             | 1               |
| Training and historic data, other periods | the observed value, or NaN if genuinely missing | 0               |
| Future data                               | not present                                     | 0               |

The indicator is named `target_masked`, not after `disease_cases`, because it marks the period rather than one variable: 1 means the target is masked in that period.

A model that ignores `target_masked` sees masked periods as missing values, so a model that already handles NaN in the target keeps working. The column lets a model tell the two kinds of NaN apart and handle masked periods on purpose. A model can:

- drop the rows where `target_masked` is 1 before fitting;
- avoid interpolating across masked periods, which can span several years;
- or keep it as a covariate. Future data always has it as 0, so the columns in history and future match, and models that fit on every column (such as an R formula `y ~ .`) or that stack historic and future data keep working.

Datasets without masked periods have no `target_masked` column, so models see exactly the same data as before. Masked periods are set when a dataset is created, or with `--data-configuration` on the command line; see the [eval command reference](https://chap.dhis2.org/chap-modeling-platform/chap-cli/eval-reference/#data-configuration).

### Requirement for Periods to be consecutive

Time periods must be consecutive with no gaps. For example, monthly data that jumps from `2023-01` to `2023-03` (skipping February) is invalid.

In addition, every location must have exactly the same set of time periods. If your dataset covers three locations over 12 months, each location must have all 12 monthly rows.

### Multi-location example

Below is a complete example showing two locations with consecutive monthly periods:

```text
time_period,location,disease_cases,rainfall,mean_temperature,population
2023-01,district_a,150,120.5,28.3,50000
2023-02,district_a,180,95.0,27.8,50000
2023-03,district_a,210,60.2,26.5,50000
2023-01,district_b,90,110.0,29.1,35000
2023-02,district_b,105,88.4,28.6,35000
2023-03,district_b,130,55.7,27.0,35000
```

### Monthly data example

```text
time_period,rainfall,mean_temperature,disease_cases,location
2023-01,10,30,200,loc1
2023-02,2,30,100,loc1
```

### Weekly data example

```text
time_period,rainfall,mean_temperature,disease_cases,location
2023-W01,12,28,45,loc1
2023-W02,8,29,52,loc1
```

### Validating your dataset

Use the `chap validate` command to check that a CSV file meets all the requirements described above before running an evaluation.

The command checks for:

- Missing or NaN values in covariate columns
- Consecutive time periods (no gaps)
- Location completeness (every location covers the same time periods)
- With `--model-name`: the covariates and period type the model requires
- With `--data-configuration`: masked ranges that fall in the evaluation window of a backtest

The command exits with code 0 when no errors are found, or code 1 if any errors are detected.

#### Validating a correct dataset

```bash
chap validate --dataset-csv example_data/laos_subset.csv
```

#### Detecting missing covariate values

```bash
chap validate --dataset-csv example_data/faulty_datasets/missing_covariate_values.csv || true
```

#### Validating against a model

To also verify that the dataset has the covariates and period type required by a specific model, pass `--model-name`:

```bash
chap validate \
    --dataset-csv example_data/laos_subset.csv \
    --model-name tests/fixture_models/naive_python_model_uv
```

#### Mapping custom column names

If your CSV uses non-standard column names, supply a mapping file with `--data-source-mapping`:

```bash
chap validate \
    --dataset-csv example_data/faulty_datasets/custom_column_names.csv \
    --data-source-mapping example_data/faulty_datasets/custom_column_names_mapping.json
```

# Defining the MLproject environment for your model

### MLproject environment

In the MLproject file you just created, you need to specify one environment Chap will run your model within. The available options are uv (Python), renv environment (for R models) and docker. Below it is described how you set up each environment.

## Option 1) uv environment (Python)

Use `uv_env` to specify a pyproject.toml for uv-managed environments. This is useful for models that use [uv](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/) for dependency management:

```yaml
uv_env: pyproject.toml
```

Commands will be executed via `uv run`, which automatically handles the virtual environment. Make sure your model directory contains a valid `pyproject.toml` with dependencies specified. See the [example uv model](https://github.com/dhis2-chap/chap-core/tree/master/tests/fixture_models/naive_python_model_uv) for a complete example.

Example MLproject file with uv

```yaml
name: my_model
uv_env: pyproject.toml
entry_points:
  train:
    parameters:
      train_data: str
      model: str
    command: "python main.py train {train_data} {model}"
  predict:
    parameters:
      model: str
      historic_data: str
      future_data: str
      out_file: str
    command: "python main.py predict {model} {historic_data} {future_data} {out_file}"
```

## Option 2) R enviroment

We reccomend to use renv to handle and specify dependenices for your R-models (link) When using renv, you only need to put this line in the ML-project file:

```yaml
renv_env: renv.lock
```

Example MLproject file with renv

```yaml
name: my_model
renv_env: renv.lock
entry_points:
  train:
    parameters:
      train_data: str
      model: str
    command: "Rscript train.R {train_data} {model}"
  predict:
    parameters:
      model: str
      historic_data: str
      future_data: str
      out_file: str
    command: "Rscript predict.R {model} {historic_data} {future_data} {out_file}"
```

A brief introduction to renv commands

1. Initialize renv in your R project:

   ```r
   renv::init()
   ```

1. Install your required packages:

   ```r
   renv::install("dplyr")
   renv::install("argparser")
   # ... other packages
   ```

1. Create the lockfile:

   ```r
   renv::snapshot()
   ```

This creates `renv.lock` with exact versions of all dependencies, ensuring reproducible environments.

See the [minimalist R model example](https://github.com/dhis2-chap/minimalist_example_renv) for a complete working example.

## Option 3) Docker environment

When UV or renv is not sufficent to reliably reproduce the environment, its also possible to spesificy a dokcer-env to run the model within.

Use `docker_env` to specify a Docker image:

For example:

```yaml
docker_env:
  image: ghcr.io/dhis2-chap/docker_r_inla
```

# Describing your model in our yaml-based format

To make your model chap-compatible, you need your train and predict endpoints (as discussed [here](https://chap.dhis2.org/chap-modeling-platform/external_models/train_and_predict/index.md)) need to be formally defined in a [YAML format](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/YAML) that follows the popular [MLflow standard](https://www.mlflow.org/docs/latest/projects.html#project-format). Your codebase need to contain a file named `MLproject`.

After adding the MLproject-file, your project typically look like this:

```text
model_folder/
├── MLproject (Add this file)
├── input (input data, e.g. disease, climate)
├── output (predcitions / evaluations)
├── train.py (or R-file)
├── predict.py (or R-file)
└── pyproject.toml (or R-file)
```

## MLproject

The MLproject file need to contain:

1. An entry point in the MLproject file called `train` with parameters `train_data` and `model`
1. An entry point in the MLproject file called `predict` with parameters `historic_data`, `future_data`, `model` and `out_file`

### Example MLproject file

Taken from our minimalist_example_uv

```yaml
name: minimalist_example_uv

uv_env: pyproject.toml

entry_points:
  train:
    parameters:
      train_data: str
      model: str
    command: "python train.py {train_data} {model}"
  predict:
    parameters:
      historic_data: str
      future_data: str
      model: str
      out_file: str
    command: "python predict.py {model} {historic_data} {future_data} {out_file}"
```

### Predict and train

When Chap runs your model, it calls the `train` and `predict` commands defined in your MLproject file. Chap creates CSV files with the data and passes their filenames as command-line arguments by substituting the `{parameter}` placeholders in the command string.

#### Train

Chap calls the `train` entry point with two parameters:

| Parameter    | Description                                            |
| ------------ | ------------------------------------------------------ |
| `train_data` | Filename of a CSV file containing the training data    |
| `model`      | Filename where your script must save the trained model |

Your train script should:

1. Read the CSV from `train_data` (columns: `time_period`, `location`, `disease_cases`, plus any covariates)
1. Fit your model on this data
1. Save the trained model to the path given by `model` (format is up to you: JSON, pickle, RDS, etc.)

**Example train script (Python):**

```python
import json
import sys
import pandas as pd

def train(training_data_filename: str, model_path: str):
    df = pd.read_csv(training_data_filename)
    stats = df.groupby("location")["disease_cases"].agg(["mean", "std"]).to_dict()
    with open(model_path, "w") as f:
        json.dump(stats, f)
```

Call the function from the command line:

```console
# train.py (bottom of file)
if __name__ == "__main__":
    train(sys.argv[1], sys.argv[2])
```

#### Predict

Chap calls the `predict` entry point with four parameters:

| Parameter       | Description                                                                  |
| --------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `historic_data` | Filename of a CSV with observed data up to the prediction period             |
| `future_data`   | Filename of a CSV with the future time periods and covariates to predict for |
| `model`         | Filename of the saved model (produced by the train step)                     |
| `out_file`      | Filename where your script must write the predictions                        |

Your predict script should:

1. Load the trained model from `model`
1. Read `historic_data` and/or `future_data` as needed
1. Generate predictions for each `(location, time_period)` row in `future_data`
1. Write a CSV to `out_file` with columns: `time_period`, `location`, `sample_0`, `sample_1`, ..., `sample_N`

Each `sample_i` column represents one draw from the predictive distribution. Chap uses these samples to compute uncertainty intervals. Typically, models produce 100 samples.

**Example predict script (Python):**

```python
import json
import sys
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

def predict(model_filename: str, historic_data_filename: str,
            future_data_filename: str, output_filename: str):
    with open(model_filename) as f:
        stats = json.load(f)

    future_df = pd.read_csv(future_data_filename)
    n_samples = 100

    rows = []
    for _, row in future_df.iterrows():
        loc = row["location"]
        mean = stats["mean"].get(loc, 0)
        std = stats["std"].get(loc, 1) or 1
        samples = np.maximum(0, np.random.normal(mean, std, n_samples))
        row_data = {"time_period": row["time_period"], "location": loc}
        row_data.update({f"sample_{i}": s for i, s in enumerate(samples)})
        rows.append(row_data)

    pd.DataFrame(rows).to_csv(output_filename, index=False)
```

Call the function from the command line:

```console
# predict.py (bottom of file)
if __name__ == "__main__":
    predict(sys.argv[1], sys.argv[2], sys.argv[3], sys.argv[4])
```

#### How parameters map to files

When Chap executes the command `"python train.py {train_data} {model}"`, it replaces `{train_data}` and `{model}` with the actual filenames of the CSV and model files it has created. Both train and predict run in the same working directory, so the model file saved during training is directly accessible during prediction.

For example, given the MLproject entry:

```yaml
command: "python predict.py {model} {historic_data} {future_data} {out_file}"
```

Chap might execute:

```console
python predict.py model.json historic_data_2024-01-01.csv future_data_2024-01-01.csv predictions_2024-01-01.csv
```

#### Optional parameters

Your MLproject entry points can also accept these optional parameters:

| Parameter      | Description                                                                                            |
| -------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| `polygons`     | Filename of a GeoJSON file with location polygon boundaries (only passed if spatial data is available) |
| `model_config` | Filename of a YAML configuration file for model-specific settings                                      |

To use these, include the corresponding `{polygons}` or `{model_config}` placeholder in your command string

# Development tools

To develop a model for Chap, you work in the terminal, get code from GitHub and install packages for your model. If these are new to you, work through the guides below in order. Each one ends with an exercise to check that it works.

1. [Working on the terminal](https://chap.dhis2.org/chap-modeling-platform/kigali-workshop/kigali-webinar-series/session-2/terminal/index.md): open a terminal, move between folders and run commands. On Windows, this includes setting up WSL.
1. [Git and GitHub](https://chap.dhis2.org/chap-modeling-platform/kigali-workshop/kigali-webinar-series/session-2/git-github/index.md): download code from GitHub and share your own.
1. [Virtual environments](https://chap.dhis2.org/chap-modeling-platform/kigali-workshop/kigali-webinar-series/session-2/virtual-environments/index.md): install the packages a project needs, with uv for Python and renv for R, without breaking other projects.

You also need an editor for your code. [RStudio](https://posit.co/download/rstudio-desktop/) is common for R, and [VS Code](https://code.visualstudio.com/) works for both R and Python.

[Docker](https://docs.docker.com/get-started/) packages a program with everything it needs, so that it runs the same on any machine. You do not need it to develop or evaluate a model, only to deploy one next to a Chap installation.

When you are comfortable with these, continue with [Set up your machine](https://chap.dhis2.org/chap-modeling-platform/external_models/setup/index.md).

# Generated Features

Chap can automatically compute derived features for your model, such as clustering locations by their seasonal disease patterns. These features are generated at runtime from the input data, so they do not need to be provided as part of the dataset.

## How It Works

You request generated features by adding entries with a `gen:` prefix to the `required_covariates` list in your MLproject file. For example:

```yaml
name: my_model

required_covariates:
  - rainfall
  - mean_temperature
  - gen:seasonality_cluster

docker_env:
  image: python:3.13

entry_points:
  train:
    parameters:
      train_data: str
      model: str
    command: "python train.py {train_data} {model}"
  predict:
    parameters:
      historic_data: str
      future_data: str
      model: str
      out_file: str
    command: "python predict.py {model} {historic_data} {future_data} {out_file}"
```

When Chap runs this model:

1. The regular covariates (`rainfall`, `mean_temperature`) are expected in the input dataset as usual
1. Generated features (`gen:seasonality_cluster`) are computed by Chap and added to the data before your model receives it
1. Your model's training and prediction data will include a `cluster_id` column alongside the regular covariates

## Available Generated Features

| Config value              | Column added | Description                                                                                                                 |
